Guided trip

Inside a neighbouring galaxy

The Large Magellanic Cloud, the Tarantula, its giant stars. Then back to Earth.

Open the trip: Inside a neighbouring galaxy

A galaxy you can see: its photograph

From the southern half of the Earth this pale cloud is plain to the eye: the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy beside ours. Stars that eclipse each other put it a hundred and sixty thousand light-years away.

Turned, it becomes a model

Off our line a model takes over. Where its stars lie on the sky comes from the Gaia spacecraft's counts; how far each sits in front or behind is a guess, as no single star's depth can be measured.

The Tarantula, inside the Cloud

The bright knot is the Tarantula Nebula, the brightest nursery of stars near us. It is part of the Large Magellanic Cloud and shares its distance; its depth within the disc is not known.

A hollow blown by young stars

Nearly two thousand light-years across, it is gas lit and pushed by young stars, whose winds have blown a hollow in its middle. Its depth here is a model; its pink hydrogen and teal oxygen are made stronger.

Home of the heaviest stars known

At its heart is R136, a cluster under two million years old whose light makes most of the nebula glow. Its brightest star is among the heaviest known, two to three hundred Suns. The stars drawn are a sample, at its real place.

Our galaxy and its neighbour

Far out, the Large Magellanic Cloud is the small patch in the middle, the Small one beside it, and our Milky Way beyond, about three times wider. Now home: a hundred and sixty thousand light-years.

Everything is drawn where it really is, from the HYG star database, OpenNGC and the planets’ own orbits (astronomy-engine).
